qs.q: Which opportunistic infection is classically associated with a CD4 count falling below 50 cells/uL?
qs.e: Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), and CNS lymphoma characteristically occur when the CD4 count drops below 50 cells/uL. Conversely, conditions like pulmonary TB or Candida vaginitis typically present at much higher CD4 counts.

qs.q: A patient with HIV presents with oral thrush and a CD4 count of 350 cells/µL. Which of the following pulmonary opportunistic infections is most characteristic of this level of immunosuppression?
qs.e: Pulmonary tuberculosis can occur across a broad range of CD4 counts including 200-500 cells/µL and even >500 cells/µL. Cytomegalovirus and Mycobacterium avium complex typically occur at much lower CD4 counts below 50 cells/µL.

qs.q: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 45 cells/µL develops a new central nervous system and pulmonary opportunistic infection. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible?
qs.e: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is classically seen in severely immunocompromised patients with a CD4 count below 50 cells/µL. Pneumocystis jirovecii typically presents when CD4 counts drop below 200 cells/µL rather than below 50.

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is classified as a direct HIV-induced lesion rather than an opportunistic infection?
qs.e: HIV encephalopathy is categorized under direct HIV-induced lesions of the central nervous system. Cryptococcal meningitis and Pneumocystis jiroveci are opportunistic infections caused by fungi.

qs.q: Which of the following fungal pathogens is part of the established spectrum of opportunistic infections in HIV/AIDS?
qs.e: Aspergillus and Candida species are listed under the spectrum of fungi affecting HIV patients. Plasmodium, microsporidia, and Leishmania are classified as parasites.

qs.q: Which group of opportunistic infections presents an increased susceptibility specifically in immunocompromised hosts?
o: Pneumocystis jiroveci, CMV, and fungal agents
Type A influenza in healthy populations
qs.e: Immunocompromised hosts have a uniquely heightened susceptibility to opportunistic agents such as Pneumocystis jiroveci, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and various fungi. Tuberculosis and influenza can affect immunocompetent individuals as well.

qs.q: Which of the following interventions is mandatory for cancer patients receiving glucocorticoid-containing chemotherapy regimens to prevent opportunistic infection?
qs.e: Patients receiving glucocorticoid-containing regimens or drugs inhibiting T cell activation must receive prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Empiric amphotericin B is reserved for persistent fever after antibacterial treatment rather than primary steroid-induced prophylaxis.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with follicular lymphoma treated with chemoimmunotherapy develops progressive cognitive decline and visual changes. MRI of the brain shows asymmetric white matter lesions without mass effect. Which underlying therapy contributed to this opportunistic infection?
o: Rituximab therapy targeting CD20 B cells
qs.e: Depletion of B cells via anti-CD20 therapy impairs humoral immunity and predisposes patients to JC virus reactivation leading to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Targeted kinase inhibitors or proteasome inhibitors do not share this specific association with JC virus reactivation.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Opportunistic infections occur when the immune system is weakened, allowing normally harmless organisms to cause disease. Clinicians must identify the underlying immune defect, recognize atypical presentations, and use targeted therapy while managing complications.

sections.p: Opportunistic infections (OIs) are infections that exploit a compromised host defense, often seen in HIV, transplant, or malignancy patients. Diagnosis combines clinical suspicion, imaging, and microbiology, guided by the patient’s immune status.
b: Identify immune defect (e.g., CD4 count, neutropenia)
Look for atypical pathogens (Pneumocystis, CMV, Toxoplasma)

t.b: Is the patient at risk for specific OIs? A count <200 cells/µL indicates high risk for Pneumocystis and cryptococcal meningitis.
Detects infiltrates suggestive of Pneumocystis or fungal pneumonia; a diffuse ground‑glass pattern raises suspicion.
Positive PCR in blood or CSF confirms CMV disease; a high viral load correlates with severity.
Positive result in serum or CSF indicates cryptococcal meningitis; a high titer predicts worse outcome.
Positive test suggests latent TB; in an immunocompromised host it may progress to active disease.

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and immune status. For example, Pneumocystis pneumonia is staged by PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio; CMV retinitis severity is staged by retinal lesion size.
b: Use WHO HIV staging for overall risk

t.b: A ratio <200 mmHg indicates severe hypoxia requiring high‑flow oxygen or ventilation.
Lesions >5 mm require urgent antiviral therapy.

sections.p: The most common causes of OIs are HIV infection, chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia, organ transplantation, and congenital immunodeficiencies. In low‑resource settings, TB, malaria, and bacterial sepsis often coexist and mask OIs.

t.b: High load correlates with rapid CD4 decline and higher OI risk.
ANC <500 cells/µL predicts bacterial and fungal infections.

sections.p: Presentation is often subtle and overlaps with common infections. Fever, weight loss, and night sweats are common, but organ‑specific signs (e.g., cough, visual changes, seizures) guide diagnosis.

t.b: Crackles or wheeze may indicate Pneumocystis or fungal pneumonia.
Cherry red spots or retinal hemorrhages suggest CMV retinitis.

sections.p: Investigation strategy prioritises rapid, affordable tests. When resources are limited, clinical algorithms and empirical therapy are essential.

t.b: Detects Plasmodium falciparum; a positive result rules out malaria as sole cause of fever.
Identifies acid‑fast bacilli in sputum; a positive result confirms TB.
Silver stain of induced sputum shows cysts; a positive result confirms PCP.
Detects HSV DNA in CSF; a positive result confirms HSV encephalitis.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid deterioration, severe hypoxia, seizures, or shock. Complications can be organ failure, secondary infections, or drug toxicity.

t.b: Hypotension indicates septic shock; requires fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.
Hypoglycaemia in a septic patient signals metabolic crisis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxia, sudden neurological decline, shock, or any sign of organ failure

faq.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV patients?
faq.a: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, especially when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/µL.

faq.q: How do I differentiate bacterial sepsis from an opportunistic infection in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Look for atypical pathogens (e.g., Pneumocystis, CMV) and consider the patient’s immune status; empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics plus targeted therapy may be needed.

faq.q: Can a patient with a low CD4 count develop malaria?
faq.a: Yes; malaria can coexist and complicate the clinical picture, so malaria testing should be done even in immunocompromised patients.
